messages.content: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape during a month.

response: The Moon appears to change shape over the course of a month because Earth observers see different amounts of the sunlit side of the Moon as it orbits Earth. When the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, the side facing us is mostly or completely dark — that's a new Moon, and it's not visible from Earth. As the Moon moves around Earth, more of its sunlit side comes into view — first a thin sliver (the first quarter), then half (the full Moon), then the second half (the last quarter), and back to a slim sliver on the other side. This cycle takes about 29.5 days, which is why we have about two Moons per month on average. The apparent size of the Moon doesn't change much — the variation in apparent size is a trick of perspective and is not noticeable to most people without comparison.

Your question is a great example of a policy decision that is not straightforward. On the one hand, AI-generated feedback can save time and produce consistent, structured responses — qualities that are genuinely valuable in a busy classroom. On the other, the accuracy of current AI systems varies, and a mistake or a tone that comes across as impersonal or incorrect can do real damage to a student's writing confidence. A useful middle path many teachers have adopted is to use AI as a first pass — checking for common errors, suggestion paragraphs, and draft structure — and then use it to prepare a second draft that is reviewed and edited by a human. This leverages AI's speed while keeping the final product accountable to a real teacher's judgment. You might also consider piloting it with a small group of students whose writing is at a similar level, to see what practical challenges arise in your specific context.

Use a commercial AI writing assistant or a dedicated educational AI tool (there are several on the market designed for school use). Spend a few weeks marking alongside the AI output, noting any patterns of error that the AI consistently misses. At the end of the pilot, bring the results — both the AI-generated feedback and your own — to a department meeting to discuss. Colleagues' experiences vary widely on this issue, and a group discussion will help build a policy that reflects the needs of your students. If the pilot shows real practical benefits, the next step would be to build it into your workflow as a tool, not a substitute for your judgment.

First, ongoing human review remains important — a system that outputs without final editing can produce feedback that is technically correct but accidentally dismissive or confusing, and it is hard to catch that without another set of eyes. Second, some students may find AI-generated feedback less personally meaningful or harder to act on, so it is worth keeping human-written feedback in the mix too. Third, the technology is improving rapidly, but outside a research context, deeper privacy questions tend to come up only when a system is deployed at scale and data is being shared broadly.
